### Observed differences

- In the later window, the elapsed time from the completion of A23 to the completion of A24 is about half of what it was: it centred on about 1.0 hours before (median 1.00, middle half roughly 0.9–1.1 hours) and centres on about 0.5 hours after (median 0.50, middle half roughly 0.45–0.55 hours), with the spread narrowing (standard deviation about 0.18 to 0.08 hours). The pair was observed in 200 of 200 traces in both windows. [TWAIT001]
- In the later window, the elapsed time from the completion of A36 to the completion of A14 is about twice what it was: about 1.0 hours before (median 1.02) versus about 2.0 hours after (median 2.02), with the spread widening (standard deviation about 0.17 to 0.28 hours). This consecutive pair was also observed less often: 200 times before versus 106 times after, i.e. in about 53 in 100 later traces. [TWAIT002]
- Both differences are extreme relative to random re-splits of the pooled data: for each item, only about 1 in 2,000 reference comparisons produced a difference this large. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a change in timing as a specific possibility: in the later window, the step between the completions of A23 and A24 takes about half as long (median about 0.5 versus 1.0 hours), while the step between the completions of A36 and A14 takes about twice as long (median about 2.0 versus 1.0 hours) and appears as a consecutive pair in about half as many traces (106 of 200 versus 200 of 200). [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Supporting signs: two time items qualified where roughly 0.01 would be expected if nothing had changed, so chance alone is a poor explanation for the set; each item rests on substantial counts (200 and 106–200 observations) and shows coherent shifts across mean, median and quartiles; both differences exceed all but about 1 in 2,000 random re-splits. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Limitations: TWAIT measures elapsed time between consecutive completion events, so the change may lie anywhere between the two completions rather than at the activities themselves; the evidence set contains no structural, ordering or participation items, so the drop in observed A36–A14 pairs cannot be attributed to participation, ordering or repetition, and the two items concern different activity pairs rather than confirming one single underlying difference. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

An important competing explanation remains for A36 and A14: a structural change — for example another activity's completion now falling between the two, or the pair simply occurring in fewer traces — could produce the same pattern alongside or instead of a pure timing change, and the timing-only evidence cannot rule this out. [TWAIT002]
